# Epistle of Barnabas — Chapter 21 (SOPHIA Consensus)

**Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas 21
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Consensus Translation

1. It is good that one who has learned the righteous judgments of the Lord, as many as are written, should walk in them. For whoever does these things will be glorified in the kingdom of God; but whoever chooses the opposite things will perish along with his works.
2. For this reason there is a resurrection; for this reason there will be a retribution. I beseech those who are in positions of honor: if you receive any of my good counsel, keep among you those from whom you may receive help — and do not neglect this.
3. The day is near in which all things will perish together with the evil one. The Lord is near, and his reward with him.
4. Again and again I urge you: be good lawgivers to one another, remain faithful counselors to one another, remove all hypocrisy from among you.
5. And may God, the Lord of the whole world, give you wisdom, understanding, insight, knowledge of his righteous ordinances, and patience.
6. Be instructed of God, seeking out what the Lord requires of you, and performing it — so that you may be found worthy on the day of judgment.
7. But if there is any recollection of what is good, remember me in meditating on these things, so that both my longing and my watching may count toward some good.
8. I ask you to grant me this request: be faithful to one another.

---

## Council Notes

- v.3: "The Lord is near, and his reward with him" — echoes Isaiah 40:10 and Revelation 22:12 ("Behold, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me"). The imminent eschatology at the close of the epistle frames the entire Two Ways teaching: the ethical urgency is grounded in the nearness of judgment.
- v.4: "Be good lawgivers to one another" — *nomothetai agathoi allelois ginesthe* — an unusual exhortation: the community is to be its own mutual legislators, each member shaping the standards for the others. This is communal ethics rather than hierarchical rule-giving.
- v.5: The closing blessing enumerates five gifts: wisdom, understanding, insight, knowledge of his ordinances, and patience. The first four echo Proverbs/Wisdom vocabulary; "patience" (*hypomonē*) is the eschatological virtue of endurance.
- v.7: "My longing and my watching" — the author's personal pastoral concern surfaces in this closing; behind the learned allegorist is a person who genuinely cares for the community's fate.
- v.8: "Be faithful to one another" — *pistoi ginesthe allelois* — the final word of the epistle is mutual faithfulness. After 20 chapters of typology, allegory, and ethical instruction, the epistle closes with the simplest and most personal request.
- Textual note: Codex Sinaiticus ends at 21:9 with what may be a scribal colophon. The Hierosolymitanus manuscript preserves a slightly variant ending.
